guide.title: EMS, Systems & Professionalism
guide.lead: An EMS system is a chain: someone recognises the emergency and calls, a dispatcher sends the right help and coaches the caller, crews treat under medical direction, hospitals take over, and quality review closes the loop. Know your link in the chain and exactly what you're authorised to do.

steps.title: Public access
steps.text: A bystander recognises the emergency and calls the emergency number (112, 911, 999 or local). Enhanced systems show the caller's location and callback number automatically.

steps.title: Dispatch
steps.text: The emergency medical dispatcher asks structured questions, sends the right resources and gives pre-arrival instructions: CPR, bleeding control, childbirth.

steps.title: Response
steps.text: First responders, then BLS and ALS crews as needed. Scene safety comes first on every call.

steps.title: Care under medical direction
steps.text: Protocols and standing orders (offline) or a physician by radio or phone (online).

steps.title: Destination
steps.text: The right hospital, not just the nearest: trauma, stroke, STEMI, burns, pediatrics.

steps.title: Quality improvement
steps.text: Review calls, find system problems, change protocols and training, measure again.

sections.title: Provider levels (US model)
rows: CPR, AED, bleeding control, basic airway, oxygen, naloxone
Adds full assessment, supraglottic airways where allowed, CPAP, some medicines (aspirin, oral glucose, epinephrine auto-injector, naloxone)
Adds IV and IO access and a few more medicines
Advanced life support: intubation, manual defibrillation, pacing, cardiac and analgesic medicines
notes: Other countries use similar tiers under different names. Your scope is set by your licence, local law and your medical director.

sections.title: Three terms that get confused
rows: What the law and your medical director authorise you to do. Going outside it is practising medicine without a licence.
What a reasonable provider with your training would do in the same situation. You can be inside scope and still below standard (right drug, wrong dose).
On duty, you must respond and care within your scope. Leaving a patient without handing over is abandonment.

groups.title: Online (direct)
items: Real-time advice from a physician by radio or phone
Needed for orders outside your standing orders

sections.title: A professional
items: Integrity: tells the truth, including about mistakes
Empathy and respect for every patient
Teamwork, clear communication and calm under stress
Patient advocacy: the patient's interest first
Physically fit, rested and well presented
Keeps learning: in the US, NREMT certification renews every 2 years

sections.title: Where EMS came from (US)
items: 1966: the white paper "Accidental Death and Disability: The Neglected Disease of Modern Society" exposed poor prehospital care
1966: the Highway Safety Act required states to build highway safety programmes, including EMS
1973: the EMS Systems Act funded regional EMS systems
Today: community paramedicine, mobile integrated health and data-driven quality improvement

quiz.q: Which 1966 publication started the modernisation of EMS in the United States?
options: "Accidental Death and Disability: The Neglected Disease of Modern Society"
The National EMS Scope of Practice Model

quiz.q: The highest of the four US EMS provider levels is:
Written orders that let you treat without calling a physician first are:
Enhanced emergency-number systems give the dispatcher:
options: The caller's location and callback number automatically
quiz.explanation: Useful when the caller can't speak.

quiz.q: Which part of the system recognises an emergency and activates it?
quiz.explanation: The bystander and the emergency number.

quiz.q: The physician responsible for an EMS system's clinical care is the:
In the US model, IV and IO access starts at which level?
Calling a physician before giving a particular drug is:
quiz.explanation: Real-time contact by radio or phone.

quiz.q: Which medicine is within the EMT scope (US model)?
The 1966 Highway Safety Act affected EMS mainly by:
options: Requiring states to build highway safety programmes, including EMS
quiz.explanation: It also created the federal transportation department's role in EMS.

quiz.q: Continuous quality improvement (CQI) in EMS is mainly about:
options: Reviewing care to find and fix system problems

quiz.q: A community paramedic would most likely:
options: Make home visits for medicine checks and chronic disease follow-up

quiz.q: Your first priority on arriving at any scene:
quiz.explanation: An injured rescuer helps no one.

quiz.q: The legal obligation of an on-duty provider to give care is:
The range of skills you are legally authorised to perform is your:
quiz.explanation: Set by law and your medical director.

quiz.q: Performing a skill outside your legal scope is:
options: Acceptable if no paramedic is available
quiz.explanation: Even if the patient does well.

quiz.q: Which best shows the difference between scope of practice and standard of care?
options: An EMT gives a drug in scope but at the wrong dose: within scope, below standard
An EMT refuses a violent patient
quiz.explanation: Scope is what you may do; standard is how well you do it.

quiz.q: How often does NREMT certification renew?

flashcards.question: The 1966 white paper
flashcards.answer: "Accidental Death and Disability: The Neglected Disease of Modern Society": exposed poor prehospital care in the US and led to EMS reform.

flashcards.question: Four US EMS provider levels
flashcards.answer: Emergency Medical Responder, EMT, Advanced EMT, Paramedic. Other countries use similar tiers.

flashcards.question: Online vs offline medical direction
flashcards.answer: Online: real-time advice from a physician by radio or phone. Offline: protocols, standing orders, training and case review.

flashcards.question: Enhanced emergency-number systems
flashcards.answer: Show the caller's location and callback number automatically, even if the caller can't speak.

flashcards.question: Continuous quality improvement
flashcards.answer: A cycle: review care, find problems, feed back, change the system, measure again. Non-punitive.

flashcards.question: 1966 Highway Safety Act
flashcards.answer: Required states to build highway safety programmes, including EMS.

flashcards.question: Emergency medical dispatcher
flashcards.answer: Answers the call, asks structured questions, sends the right resources and gives pre-arrival instructions (CPR, bleeding control).

flashcards.question: EMT vs paramedic scope
flashcards.answer: EMT: basic life support – assessment, bleeding control, basic and supraglottic airways, CPAP, limited medicines. Paramedic: advanced life support – intubation, IV/IO, manual defibrillation, pacing, advanced medicines.

flashcards.question: Scope of practice vs standard of care
flashcards.answer: Scope: what you are legally allowed to do. Standard: what a reasonable provider with your training would do in the same situation.

flashcards.question: Duty to act
flashcards.answer: On duty you must respond and care within your scope. Ending care without handing over to an equal or higher provider is abandonment.

flashcards.question: National certification (US)
flashcards.answer: The National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (NREMT); renews every 2 years. Licensing is by the state.

flashcards.question: First action on every scene
flashcards.answer: Scene safety: for you, your partner, the patient and bystanders.

flashcards.question: Traits of a professional
flashcards.answer: Integrity, empathy, respect, teamwork, communication, calm under stress, patient advocacy, fitness, lifelong learning.

critical.scenario: Rural crash: an unconscious driver found by a passer-by. The dispatcher stayed on the line and coached the caller to open the airway and press on an arm wound. You're 20 minutes from a community hospital and 45 from a trauma centre.
critical.question: The dispatcher's coaching is an example of:

options.t: Emergency medical dispatch giving pre-arrival instructions

critical.explanation: Dispatchers turn bystanders into the first link of care.
critical.kpi: Identifies the role of emergency medical dispatch in the EMS system

critical.scenario: Your medical director adds CPAP for respiratory distress without needing to call. A 68-year-old with crackles and SpO₂ 88% improves to 94% on CPAP.
critical.question: Treating without calling a physician is:

options.t: Offline medical direction through a standing order

critical.explanation: Standing orders are written in advance by the medical director.
critical.kpi: Distinguishes online from offline medical direction

critical.scenario: A case review finds a ROSC patient went to a hospital without a cath lab and had to be transferred. Protocols had no post-arrest destination rule. A new rule sends ROSC patients to a PCI centre, adding 8 minutes of transport.
critical.question: What does this show about CQI?

options.t: It finds system problems and makes evidence-based changes

options.f: No one was at fault: the protocol was missing.

options.t: It reduces transport times at all costs
options.f: The new rule adds time to save more.

critical.explanation: Good CQI fixes systems, not people.

critical.scenario: During a transfer, a patient with a valid DNR you have seen goes into cardiac arrest. Your experienced partner says 'just start CPR – nobody checks the paperwork'.
critical.question: Most professional decision?

options.t: Honour the valid DNR, give comfort care, and explain your decision to your partner
Follow your partner because they're more experienced
options.f: Experience doesn't override the patient's legal wishes.
Ignoring a valid DNR is a breach of the patient's rights.

critical.explanation: Document the DNR and the time of death per protocol.
critical.kpi: Honors a valid DNR order under peer pressure

critical.scenario: Minor crash: a 35-year-old driver denies injury, is upset, must get to work, refuses assessment and signing, and walks away.
critical.question: Most professional approach?

options.t: Explain the risks if she will listen, then document her refusal, what you told her, and that she left without signing

options.f: That's false imprisonment if she has capacity.
Not without a reason she lacks capacity.

critical.kpi: Manages and documents a refusal from a patient who leaves
